findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness and distractibility; observed events with closed eyes, asynchronous movements and pelvic thrusting
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs and observe an event
action_criteria.rationale: Five days of right leg weakness and shaking events: the diagnosis rests on positive signs such as the Hoover sign and collapsing weakness and on the semiology of observed events, not on the exclusion of other disease (DSM-5 criterion B).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No diffusion restriction and no demyelinating lesion on a non-contrast study
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast for the stroke and demyelination question
action_criteria.rationale: The outside team considered stroke or demyelination for abrupt right leg weakness and gave empirical dexamethasone, and she had episodes of limb weakness in her twenties. One non-contrast MRI with diffusion answers that question once; gadolinium adds nothing to it.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Record the habitual events on video-EEG
action_criteria.rationale: She was given lorazepam for presumed seizures. Recording her habitual events without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level of certainty and assesses co-occurring epilepsy before benzodiazepines and antiseizure drugs are ruled out, as the AAN guideline advises. Without the recording, the positive signs and the semiology of witnessed events support the diagnosis at a lower ILAE level of certainty (LaFrance 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: As-needed clonazepam identified as a benzodiazepine not to be used for the events; bleeding risk of escitalopram with naproxen
action_criteria.label: Review the current medicines, including the as-needed clonazepam
action_criteria.rationale: She takes clonazepam as needed and was given lorazepam for the events elsewhere; benzodiazepine rescue reinforces an epileptic model and sedates. Escitalopram with naproxen adds a bleeding risk.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies mood, anxiety and symptom burden to guide therapy; does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment, if it will guide therapy
action_criteria.rationale: It can quantify her depression, anxiety and trauma-related symptoms to target psychological treatment, but it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway, so it is justified only when the result will shape therapy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background evidence only, with no bearing on this patient's work-up
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on FND diagnosis and treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Reading on positive signs and treatment trials is background knowledge, not a clinical step; nothing in this patient's diagnosis or plan depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
Continue or restart empirical corticosteroids for presumed demyelination or stroke.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (mixed: functional right leg weakness and functional seizures) based on the right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness and distractibility, the semiology of the observed events, confirmed on video-EEG where recorded, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid recurrent major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Do not use her as-needed clonazepam to abort the events; review it with her prescriber and taper it gradually as her anxiety treatment allows.

avoided_actions.rationale: She has no syncope, murmur or embolic question, and the events are shaking with retained awareness; an echocardiogram answers nothing.
The events are 2 to 4 minutes of shaking during which she remains aware, with no syncope or palpitations; nothing suggests an arrhythmia.
The non-contrast MRI is the study for her stroke and demyelination question; a head CT adds radiation and no information.
Demyelination was considered, but she is afebrile with no infective prodrome, and the positive signs and a normal MRI leave no question for a lumbar puncture, which would add iatrogenic risk.
FDG-PET has no diagnostic role in functional seizures or functional weakness and answers no question in this patient.

The right leg weakness has normal reflexes, tone and bulk with a positive Hoover sign and collapsing weakness; it is not neuromuscular, and a normal EMG would only feed the search for an organic cause.
Sensory loss of the whole right leg ending at the inguinal crease, with intact vibration and proprioception, is not a question about the somatosensory pathway.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) with functional limb weakness and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures

differential.key_features: Generalized shaking episodes treated as seizures at the outside hospital. Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures.

Abrupt right leg weakness raised stroke at the outside hospital; symmetric reflexes, flexor plantars, a positive Hoover sign and collapsing weakness, and no restricted diffusion on MRI argue against it.

Leg weakness with sensory symptoms and resolved episodes of limb weakness in her twenties raise demyelination; normal reflexes, intact vibration and proprioception, positive functional signs and no white matter lesion on MRI argue against it.

A sensory boundary at the inguinal crease can suggest a level, but the light-touch and pinprick loss is on the same side as the weakness with intact vibration and proprioception, the reverse of a hemicord pattern, and reflexes, plantars and bladder function are normal; this does not fit a cord lesion.

key_clinical_evidence: The right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness and distractibility (near-normal use of the leg while adjusting her seated position) are validated rule-in signs; the sensory loss ending at the inguinal crease and better movement when unobserved are supportive only.

The observed events have closed eyes resisting opening, asynchronous limb movements, pelvic thrusting and immediate recovery, and two habitual events were recorded on video-EEG without ictal change: the ILAE documented level of certainty.
One non-contrast MRI with diffusion answers the stroke and demyelination question raised at the outside hospital; gadolinium and repeat imaging add nothing.
Benzodiazepines are not a treatment for functional seizures: the outside lorazepam and her as-needed clonazepam should not be used to abort the events (AAN 2025).
The argument with her husband, the threat of job loss, childhood emotional trauma, depression and anxiety are supportive context; a stressor is neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Generalized anxiety disorder and recurrent major depressive disorder
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions (MS, migraine, epilepsy) also flare with stress. Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive rule-in signs.
red_herrings.data_point: Abrupt onset after an argument with her husband about losing her job
red_herrings.intended_effect: Make the diagnosis from the stressor alone, without positive signs or typical event semiology

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Treatment given on a presumption is not evidence for it: the habitual events recorded without ictal change and the normal MRI answer both questions.
red_herrings.data_point: Lorazepam for presumed seizures and empirical intravenous dexamethasone at the outside hospital
red_herrings.intended_effect: Take the outside treatment as evidence of epilepsy or demyelination and continue benzodiazepines, antiseizure drugs or steroids

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Relapsing episodes raise MS, but the examination is incompatible with a central lesion and the MRI shows no demyelinating lesion; earlier functional episodes are common in FND.
red_herrings.data_point: Episodes of unexplained limb weakness in her twenties that resolved spontaneously
red_herrings.intended_effect: Read relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis into the history and pursue a demyelination work-up

sequence_constraints.reason: The examination comes first: its positive signs decide whether imaging has a specific question to answer (Espay 2018).

findings.result: Right hip extension weak on direct testing, full strength during left hip flexion against resistance.
Right hip flexion and knee extension collapse on formal testing, to an apparent 2/5.
She uses the right leg with near-normal strength while adjusting her seated position, and the dragging gait varies during observation.

Two episodes of generalized shaking lasting 2 to 3 minutes, with the eyes closed and resisting opening, asynchronous limb movements and pelvic thrusting, followed by immediate recovery without confusion.

Light-touch and pinprick loss over the whole right leg ending sharply at the inguinal crease, more fluid movement when she believes she is unobserved, and exaggerated Romberg sway without falling; not counted as rule-in signs.
Reflexes 2+ and symmetric with flexor plantars and no clonus; normal bulk and tone; vibration and proprioception intact.
findings.sign: Reflexes, tone and posterior column sensation

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness and distractibility of the right leg deficit. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion. The event semiology (eyes closed and resisting opening, asynchronous limb movements, pelvic thrusting, immediate recovery without confusion) is typical of functional seizures; the examination does not by itself exclude epileptic seizures.

interactions: Escitalopram with naproxen: SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin and NSAIDs injure the gastric mucosa; increased risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Consider gastroprotection or a non-NSAID analgesic.
Escitalopram with clonazepam: additive central nervous system depression; minor.
current_medications.proposed: Escitalopram 20 mg once daily; clonazepam 0.5 mg twice daily as needed; naproxen 500 mg twice daily as needed
current_medications.summary: Escitalopram with naproxen raises the gastrointestinal bleeding risk; clonazepam adds sedation and carries benzodiazepine cautions.
warnings: Clonazepam: sedation, tolerance and dependence; avoid using a benzodiazepine as rescue for paroxysmal events not shown to be epileptic, and after regular use taper gradually rather than stopping abruptly.
Escitalopram: dose-dependent QTc prolongation; 20 mg daily is the maximum recommended dose.

activating_procedures.hyperventilation: Performed for 3 minutes. No activation of epileptiform activity. No clinical events provoked.
activating_procedures.photic_stimulation: Performed at standard flash frequencies. Normal photic driving response. No photoparoxysmal response.

artifacts.description: During both events, partially obscuring the tracing; the underlying background remained interpretable between bursts.

background.continuity: Continuous background without suppressions or discontinuity
background.overall: Continuous inpatient video-EEG for 48 hours, international 10-20 system with a single-lead ECG channel. Normal, symmetric background in wakefulness and sleep.
background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: 10 Hz symmetric alpha rhythm, well-regulated and reactive to eye opening
background.sleep_features: Normal sleep architecture; vertex waves and sleep spindles in stage N2 sleep

findings.morphology: Generalized shaking with asynchronous limb movements and pelvic thrusting, eyes closed, lasting 2 min 20 s. Movement artifact over all channels at the peak; the posterior alpha rhythm remained visible between artifact bursts. No evolving rhythmic activity and no postictal slowing.

Asynchronous shaking of all four limbs with the eyes held closed against the technologist's attempt to open them, lasting 3 min 05 s. Posterior alpha rhythm persisted between artifact bursts; no evolving rhythmic activity and no postictal slowing.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. Two habitual events were recorded (generalized asynchronous shaking with the eyes closed, 2 min 20 s and 3 min 05 s) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the events; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the events. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures.
eeg.limitations: Movement artifact partially obscured the tracing during the events.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

patient.history_present_illness: A 40-year-old right-handed woman presents as an inpatient transfer from an outside hospital with a 5-day history of progressive right leg weakness and episodic generalized shaking episodes. Symptoms began abruptly following a heated argument with her husband regarding potential job termination. She initially noticed difficulty walking, with her right leg feeling heavy and dragging. Over the ensuing days, the weakness progressed to the point where she required a wheelchair for mobility. She also developed episodes of uncontrollable whole-body shaking, during which she remains aware of her surroundings but feels unable to control the movements. She reports having had approximately six such episodes over the past five days, each lasting two to four minutes, with complete return to her baseline between events. At the outside hospital, she was treated with lorazepam for presumed seizures, and there was consideration of a possible stroke or demyelinating disease given the acuity of her symptoms. She was started on intravenous dexamethasone empirically but showed no improvement in her leg weakness after two days. She denies any preceding febrile illness, recent travel, tick bites, new back pain, bowel or bladder incontinence, visual changes, numbness or tingling in other limbs, difficulty swallowing, or speech difficulties. She reports significant emotional distress related to her current life circumstances and has been experiencing poor sleep and reduced appetite for the past several weeks. She acknowledges a history of similar but less severe episodes of unexplained limb weakness in her twenties that resolved spontaneously. She denies any head trauma.

neurological_exam.additional: Hoover sign positive on the right: right hip extension is weak on direct testing, but full-strength involuntary right hip extension is felt during resisted left hip flexion. Tremor entrainment not tested (no tremor present). During two witnessed episodes of generalized shaking resembling seizures, patient maintained eye closure with resistance to opening, had asynchronous limb movements, and pelvic thrusting was noted. Episodes lasted 2-3 minutes with immediate return to baseline consciousness and no post-ictal confusion.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing normal bilaterally. Heel-to-shin testing normal on left; patient reports unable to perform on right due to weakness, but when leg passively placed shows no dysmetria.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial sensation intact to light touch bilaterally. Facial movements symmetric. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient drags right leg with exaggerated hip circumduction; however, gait pattern is inconsistent and variable during observation. When patient believes she is not being observed, right leg movement appears more fluid. Romberg testing shows dramatic sway without falling, with consistent self-correction.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Appears distressed and tearful. Speech is fluent without dysarthria or aphasia. Attention and concentration intact. Memory grossly intact for immediate and short-term recall.
neurological_exam.motor: Right lower extremity: give-way weakness with collapsing pattern on formal strength testing (apparent 2/5 hip flexion and knee extension); however, when distracted during seated position adjustment, patient uses right leg with near-normal strength. Left lower extremity 5/5 throughout. Upper extremities 5/5 bilaterally. Muscle bulk and tone normal in all extremities. No tremor at rest or with action.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally. Triceps 2+ bilaterally. Brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 2+ bilaterally. Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the entire right lower extremity with a sharp non-dermatomal demarcation at the inguinal crease. Vibration and proprioception intact bilaterally. Sensation in upper extremities normal.
